title: Formal US democratic protections persist while institutional functioning and oversight weaken
source_unit: Freedom House Freedom in the World 2026 United States country assessment of political rights and civil liberties during 2025
geography: United States; federal political institutions, elections, civil liberties, media, courts, and affected population groups

observations.period: 2025 assessment published 2026; aggregate political-rights and civil-liberties score
observations.method: Expert-coded Freedom House assessment using political-rights and civil-liberties indicators aggregated into a 100-point country score.
observations.uncertainty: An expert-coded index compresses heterogeneous legal and institutional developments; a score change does not measure every person's lived rights or establish a single cause.
observations.subgroup: US voters, political opposition, media, civil society, universities, immigrants, racial and ethnic minorities, and other groups whose rights or access may differ from the national assessment.
observations.counterinterpretation: The country remained classified Free, elections were generally competitive, courts blocked some executive actions, and formal speech and religious protections remained strong; decline is not equivalent to democratic collapse.

observations.period: 2025; functioning of government and legislative-executive balance

functioning_score.unit: Freedom House C1 score out of 4

prior_functioning_score.unit: prior-year Freedom House C1 score out of 4

government_shutdown.unit: days in the longest federal shutdown in US history, as reported by Freedom House

observations.method: Freedom House country narrative and indicator scoring on legislative capacity, appropriations, executive authority, and institutional checks.
observations.uncertainty: The score and narrative combine legal interpretation, political events, and institutional assessment; counts of orders or votes do not alone measure policy quality, implementation, or constitutional validity.
observations.subgroup: Congress, executive agencies, courts, states, public-service users, and communities affected by funding interruptions or administrative changes.
observations.counterinterpretation: The separation of powers and judicial review remained active, and some executive actions were blocked; institutional conflict can be a sign of contestation as well as dysfunction.

anticorruption_score.unit: Freedom House C2 score out of 4

prior_anticorruption_score.unit: prior-year Freedom House C2 score out of 4

inspectors_general_removed.unit: inspectors general removed in January 2025 according to the report

specialized_corruption_prosecutors.value: career lawyers in the Department of Justice specialized political-corruption unit fell from 36 to 2

observations.method: Freedom House country assessment of ethics rules, oversight bodies, enforcement, conflicts of interest, and anticorruption safeguards.
observations.uncertainty: The report records institutional actions and assessment judgments but does not establish that any named action caused corruption, financial loss, or a particular enforcement outcome.
observations.subgroup: Inspectors general, whistleblowers, public-integrity investigators, agencies, contractors, political donors, and members of the public relying on oversight.
observations.counterinterpretation: Formal safeguards, courts, Congress, journalism, and civil society continued to create avenues for challenge; staffing or leadership changes do not by themselves prove oversight failure.

denominator.unit: Freedom House D4 score range for freedom of expression

expression_score.unit: Freedom House D4 score out of 4

prior_expression_score.unit: prior-year Freedom House D4 score out of 4

protest_scale.value: No Kings protests occurred in more than 2,000 locations in June, with an estimated five million participants

press_violence.value: 35 journalists arrested and 188 assaulted in 2025 according to the US Press Freedom Tracker figures cited by the report

observations.method: Freedom House assessment of speech, protest, media pressure, surveillance, reprisals, and civic participation, supplemented by cited event and press-freedom data.
observations.uncertainty: Event counts and country scoring do not measure the prevalence of self-censorship, the legality of every incident, or the causal effect of government action on civic participation.
observations.subgroup: Journalists, protesters, citizens, noncitizens, immigrants, political opponents, and communities exposed to surveillance, intimidation, or political violence.
observations.counterinterpretation: Large peaceful protests and continued media pluralism demonstrate civic capacity and resilience even while the report identifies chilling effects and institutional pressure.

related_sources.claim: The country page links the full Freedom in the World 2026 report and methodology context.

boundary: This record adds a US institutional-functioning route linking democratic status, legislative capacity, executive oversight, anticorruption safeguards, expression, protest, and civic resilience. It is an expert-coded country assessment with cited event evidence, not a causal political-behavior study, legal ruling, or complete measure of lived rights.
